newsitem.title: JAPAN: Ex-copper star Hamanaka's family raises bail money.
newsitem.headline: Ex-copper star Hamanaka's family raises bail money.

text.p: Former star copper trader Yasuo Hamanaka, on trial for the largest trading scandal in history, relied on his relatives to raise 50 million yen ($409,000) in bail money to get him out of jail, his lawyers said on Tuesday.
"He is pleased with being granted bail of 50 million yen. This was much cheaper and quicker than he had expected," said Hidesato Sekine, one of three lawyers for Hamanaka.
Sekine said Hamanaka collected the bail money from his relatives, and said his former employer, Sumitomo Corp, was not involved in raising the funds.
Hamanaka, 49, pleaded guilty last week to fraud and forgery in connection with unauthorised trades over a decade that cost Sumitomo $2.6 billion. He was fired by the company last June.
The charges carry a penalty of up to 15 years in prison and the defence has said it plans to introduce evidence showing Hamanaka was not completely to blame for the massive losses.
Hamanaka is now quietly awaiting his second court hearing on March 10, Sekine said.
After almost four months in jail, Hamanaka has lost weight, he said. "He was dieting in jail, eating only about half the meals and doing exercises."
Sekine said Hamanaka is just hoping the trial will end as quickly as possible so he can get on with his life.
"He said that living in jail was healthy, because there are no cigarettes or alcohol around. He is trying to think about his life positively," the lawyer said.

On Monday evening the one-time copper king returned to his two-storey house in the city of Kawasaki, on the outskirts of Tokyo, an average home in a neighbourhood populated by ordinary office workers rather than financial superstars.
Hamanaka's trading activities, which earned him the nickname "Mr Five Percent" for the control he wielded, are also under investigation by regulators in both Britain and the United States.

Traders have claimed over the years that Hamanaka kept copper prices artificially high through skilful use of complex derivatives transactions and his iron grip on a large amount of copper stocks in London Metal Exchange warehouses.
But his lawyers said claims of price manipulation had nothing to do with the trial in Tokyo.
"We're dealing with charges of fraud and forgery. That allegation has nothing to do with it," said Toru Yoshiki, another lawyer on Hamanaka's defence team.
Japanese prosecution sources said earlier they had given U.S. and British regulators transcripts of their questioning of Hamanaka.
Japanese authorities contend that since the trades took place overseas, they are not involved in trying to determine if Hamanaka or Sumitomo tried to manipulate the world copper market.
